text: People don't quit the game. They quit organizing it. Six messages, and still no game.
This is Serve, built during this hackathon. Your agent works out your week with your friends' agents; you say yes once. It runs on Muse Glimmer, on my own RTX 3090.

Act one: cold start. I ask my agent for one more player on Saturday. Muse Glimmer drafts the invite with the nearest court, and Llama Guard checks it before anyone sees it. I post it, and share the link to any group chat.
Leo has no account. The link opens the game, one sign-in, and he's in. The game is full, and I hear: game on.

Act two: agents negotiate. One tap plans my week. My agent talks to each member's agent over A2A, with signed Agent Cards; in this demo club, the members are simulated. The plan took 78 seconds, in the background. Everyone agreed, and nothing is booked until I say yes.
Or in Messenger: one yes, and it's booked.
And it's a real negotiation: Hana's agent counter-offers Saturday.

Act three: courts and clubs. Real courts from OpenStreetMap. Prompt Guard screens the reviews first, then Glimmer judges every court, and each reason cites the map, a review or the forecast. Clubs sit on a real map too, and anyone can start one.
Beyond text: send a video, like this sample clip, and it's auto-cut into a clip to share with your club.
Six Meta models carry Serve, with Muse Glimmer at the center.
Glimmer needs forty seconds. The 1B model I fine-tuned on its choices needs under one, and agrees with it 89.5 percent of the time.
Ninety-three scripted attacks, all stopped, and 37 of 42 unsafe messages refused.
It's live: eight people so far, me included, and three games filled.
And it works for school clubs, older adults, a charity cup: any ball sport.
